newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin moves to sanatorium, sacks sports chief.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin moves to sanatorium, sacks sports chief.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, facing open heart surgery in the next two months, has moved from hospital to a sanatorium near Moscow where he can increase his workload, the presidential press office said on Monday.
The press service also announced that Yeltsin had formally dismissed one-time confidant and tennis coach Shamil Tarpishchev as Russia's sports chief.
The decision, which television channels reported at the weekend, heightened talk of infighting in Yeltsin's entourage amid trading of corruption charges.
A brief Kremlin statement said Yeltsin's doctors had recommended he move to the Barvikha sanatorium. "The condition of the Russian president is quite satisfactory," it said.
A spokesman said Yeltsin, 65, would be able to increase his workload and be more physically active at Barvikha, a compound of government dachas and sanatoria in woodland outside Moscow.
Yeltsin arrived at the sanatorium at the weekend and had talks there on Monday with Yegor Stroyev, the head of the Federation Council upper house of parliament.

The Kremlin said there were no plans to change the timeframe for Yeltsin's heart operation, which will graft in new veins to bypass blocked coronary arteries and improve the supply of blood to his heart.

Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and doctors say he may have had a third just before the second round of the Russian presidential election on July 3, in which he defeated a communist candidate.
He announced on September 5 that he would have a heart operation and had been in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital since September 13 while doctors prepared him for the operation.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin will assume Yeltin's official duties during the operation and has already been handed some of the president's functions.

Interfax news agency said Chernomyrdin discussed Yeltsin's planned operation by telephone on Monday with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl. The agency said Chernomyrdin had confirmed Russia's readiness to use the services of two German doctors as advisers in a conversation lasting about 40 minutes.
Although Yeltsin has said Chernomoyrdin will deputise for him, jostling for power and influence is widely thought to have intensified in the president's absence.

Talk of infighting mounted with the removal of Tarpishchev as chairman of the State Committee on Sports and Tourism. The Kremlin gave no for explain his dismissal, which takes effect on November 1, saying only that he was being moved to another job.
A former tennis professional, Tarpishchev rose to power through his friendship with Yeltsin and Alexander Korzhakov, who was sacked as head of the president's personal security in June.
In a further sign of manoeuvring for position, Korzhakov was also under fire on Monday.

Boris Fyodorov, the former head of the National Sports Fund, accused Korzhakov in two separate television interviews of trying to extort $40 million from the Fund, which used a lucrative tax break to import alcohol and tobacco free of duty.
Korzhakov could not be reached for comment. He is not charged with any offence.
The timing of the charge suggested an attempt to block any political alliance between Korzhakov and security tsar Alexander Lebed, who has not concealed his presidential ambitions.

Lebed met NATO leaders in Brussels on Monday. He cautioned them against hasty expansion eastwards, which Moscow fears will threaten its security interests, but signalled that Russia would not "go into hysterics", whatever NATO did.
